Well, doc, to be honest, I'm mostly here because my wife finally put her foot down, and my shift supervisor at the plant isn't exactly thrilled with me right now either. It’s... well, what really brought me in is that everybody keeps saying I’m not listening to them. And I mean, I *am* trying to listen.

I don't know, a minute goes by, they finish talking, and I suddenly realize I only caught maybe half of what they said. It's like the audio just cuts out in my brain halfway through the sentence.

And at work, you know, you really can't be doing that—you can't have the boss repeating himself three times about safety protocols or quotas because I just lost the back half of the conversation while staring right at him. People think I just don't care or I'm ignoring them on purpose, but I'm really not. I just... I completely miss it, and it's causing a lot of problems for me right now.

Like at the plant, they have these spec sheets for every single run we do. Dave—my supervisor, the one with the yellow glasses—he'll pin the work order to the clipboard right at my station. It’s got all the tolerances, the material codes, the exact pressure settings for the stamping press, how many units per bundle, all of that. I can read that sheet, punch the settings into the machine, and I am good to go. I never mess up the written specs. If it's on paper, I can just look at it, process it, and do exactly what it says. 

It’s the exact same deal with the truck. That transmission rebuild I was telling you about on the Silverado? I actually went online and tracked down the official OEM service manual for it. It’s this massive book, honestly thicker than an old phone directory. It’s got all these crazy exploded diagrams and step-by-step tear-down instructions for the gear trains and the clutch packs. I can sit out there in the garage with a greasy thumb, trace the lines on the schematic, read the exact torque specs for the valve body bolts, and follow it to the letter. And I mean, you really have to pay attention to that stuff, right? Because if you torque a steel bolt to 15 foot-pounds when the manual says 10, you’re gonna strip out the aluminum housing, and then you are really up a creek. You'd have to drill it out, tap a new thread, put in a helicoil... it's a nightmare. So I read every single line of that manual very carefully. Never had a single issue understanding it. 

So yeah, reading instructions, following a list, a manual, a blueprint... totally fine. My brain processes all that perfectly. It’s just... like I was saying before, it’s when someone opens their mouth and expects me to just catch the words out of the air. If my wife would just text me a grocery list or write it on a Post-it note, I’d get every single item, no problem. But if she just tells me as I’m walking out the door? Forget it, I'll come back with milk and completely forget the other five things. But the reading part itself? No, I'm a hundred percent fine with written instructions. Always have been.

No, podcasts are actually totally fine. I don't have any trouble with them at all. It's funny you bring that up, actually, because I listen to them constantly. Like, every single day. 

When I’m driving to the plant—it’s about a forty-minute commute if I take the county highway, depending on if they’ve got that construction going on near the river bridge, which they usually do these days, just bumper-to-bumper nonsense—but anyway, I always throw on a podcast. Plus, if I did somehow miss a second because I dropped a wrench or something, I can just tap my phone and hit that button that jumps back fifteen seconds, right? But honestly, I usually don't even need to. It just flows right in. 

So yeah, audio stuff, listening to things on my phone or the radio while I'm moving around? Absolutely no problem at all. I actually prefer it, to be honest with you. It gives my brain something to chew on while my hands are doing the heavy lifting.

I can sit out there in the garage with a greasy thumb, trace the lines on the schematic, read the exact torque specs for the valve body bolts, and follow it to the letter. And I mean, you really have to pay attention to that stuff, right? Because if you torque a steel bolt to 15 foot-pounds when the manual says 10, you’re gonna strip out the aluminum housing, and then you are really up a creek. You'd have to drill it out, tap a new thread, put in a helicoil... it's a nightmare. So I read every single line of that manual very carefully. Never had a single issue understanding it. \n\nSo yeah, reading instructions, following a list, a manual, a blueprint... totally fine. My brain processes all that perfectly. It’s just... like I was saying before, it’s when someone opens their mouth and expects me to just catch the words out of the air. If my wife would just text me a grocery list or write it on a Post-it note, I’d get every single item, no problem. But if she just tells me as I’m walking out the door? Forget it, I'll come back with milk and completely forget the other five things. But the reading part itself? No, I'm a hundred percent fine with written instructions. Always have been.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble remembering things that happened recently?\n\nPatient: No, not at all. My memory is actually really sharp. If something happens, it's locked in there. You know, I really haven't noticed anything like that. Not at all. It doesn't seem to matter if they're whispering or shouting or if they're from the other side of the world, to tell you the truth.

You'd have to drill it out, tap a new thread, put in a helicoil... it's a nightmare. So I read every single line of that manual very carefully. You know, I wish I could say it was just the complicated stuff, because then I’d at least have an excuse, right? Like, if somebody is throwing a bunch of technical jargon at me, it would make sense to lose track. Honestly? No. I mean, you’d think maybe I’d tune out more if it was boring, or maybe pay better attention if it was serious and emotional, but it really doesn’t change a thing. It’s the exact same problem. 

Like, just a couple weeks ago, my buddy Steve—he runs the forklift over on the midnight shift, we’ve been fishing together up at Houghton Lake for probably fifteen years now—anyway, Steve is going through this really, really ugly divorce. And I want to be a good friend, I really do. I care about the guy. I’m sitting there across the table, leaning in, looking him right in the eye, telling myself, pay attention, this is important, Steve needs you right now. And for the first sentence or two, I’m right there with him. But then... it just happens again. The exact same way it happens with the lockout/tagout binder or the recycling bin. He’s talking, and he’s clearly upset, and I can see his mouth moving, but the words just turn into complete static in my head. I end up just having to nod and say, man, that's rough, I'm so sorry, because I completely lost the thread of what he was actually crying about. 

It makes you feel like an absolute jerk, to be honest with you. Sitting there completely losing track of the conversation while your best friend is spilling his guts. But it’s not because it’s emotional or personal that I lose track, and it's not any worse than when it's about sports or work. It’s just... the exact same wall I hit with everything else. The topic could be his broken heart or a broken spark plug, and my brain just drops it exactly the same way. So no, the emotional stuff doesn't make it any harder to understand, but it sure doesn't make it any easier either.

Doc, I gotta laugh, because I feel like you're digging for some kind of medical, scientific loophole here, and I'm just sitting here sounding like a broken record.
